You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a launch announcement of up to 500 words for a new feature of a B2B helpdesk product: a Slack integration that posts a daily summary of open support tickets to a channel of the customer's choice. The audience is existing customers.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
Hey team. We just shipped a Slack integration a bunch of you have asked for over the past few months. Once a day it posts a short summary of your open support tickets into whatever channel you choose. That’s it. No extra dashboards, no new place to check. Just a quiet recap so the people who live in Slack can see what’s still waiting without opening the helpdesk first thing.

You pick the channel. You pick the time that makes sense for your team. The post itself is simple: how many tickets are still open, a quick split by priority if you use it, a handful of the oldest ones so nothing sits too long, and a link back if someone wants to jump in. We kept it light on purpose. The goal is to meet you where you already are, not to turn Slack into another ticket queue.

A lot of you told us tickets get lost in the shuffle when half the company never leaves chat. This doesn’t replace the helpdesk. It just gives the rest of the team a daily pulse so fewer things fall through. If your morning standup already happens in Slack, now the open-ticket picture is sitting right there.

To turn it on, go into settings, connect Slack, choose the channel, and you’re done. It takes a couple of minutes. We’re starting with the daily summary and we’ll listen to how you actually use it before we pile on more.

Thanks for sticking with us. Let us know how it feels once it’s running.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Starting today, you can connect your helpdesk to Slack and get a daily summary of your open tickets posted right in the channel of your choosing.

We built this because of a pattern we kept hearing in support calls. Teams love having a single place where tickets live, but most of the day happens somewhere else, usually Slack. So people were either keeping a browser tab pinned all day or, more often, wandering into the queue mid afternoon and discovering something had been sitting untouched since Monday. A daily nudge in the place you already work seemed like the smallest possible fix for a genuinely annoying problem.

Here is what the summary includes. You get a count of tickets currently open, broken out by status, plus the number that came in since the last summary and the number that were resolved. Under that, you get the tickets that need attention most: anything past its first response target, anything with no owner, and your oldest open items. Each one links straight back to the ticket, so someone can claim it without hunting for it. If your queue is quiet, the message says so and stays short.

Setup takes about two minutes. Go to Settings, then Integrations, and choose Slack. You will be asked to authorize the connection, then pick a channel. We would suggest a channel your support team already reads rather than creating a new one, since new channels tend to get muted within a week. From there you can set the delivery time, choose the time zone it should follow, and decide which days it posts. Plenty of teams turn off weekends. You can also filter the summary by team, queue, or priority, which is useful if you have separate groups handling billing and technical issues and do not want one flooding the other's channel.

A few notes worth knowing. You can connect more than one channel, each with its own filters and schedule, so a team lead can get a wide view while individual squads see only their own work. The integration reads from your existing permissions, so it will not surface anything a person could not already see in the app. And if you want to check the queue outside the daily post, you can type a slash command in Slack and get the current numbers on demand.

This is a first version and we know there are obvious next steps. Real time alerts for high priority tickets, threaded replies so discussion stays attached to a ticket, and the ability to reply to a customer from Slack are all things we have heard requested and are looking at. Weekly and monthly rollups are on the list too. If one of those matters more than the others for your team, tell us, because that is largely how we will decide the order.

The integration is available now on all plans at no extra cost. There is a short setup guide in the help center with screenshots if you would rather follow along, and our support team is happy to walk through it with you if you would like a hand choosing filters.

As always, we would rather hear what is not working than not hear it. Send us a note.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_A: Negative parallelism used twice as a rhetorical device ('meet you where you already are, not to turn Slack into...', 'This doesn’t replace the helpdesk. It just gives...') (Tell 1)
Relentless short punchy fragments creating a staccato cadence ('That’s it.', 'No extra dashboards, no new place to check.', 'You pick the channel. You pick the time...') (Tell 9)
Performing for an imagined crowd with vague generalities and no concrete details for many sentences in a row (Tell 15)
Over-explaining inferences ('We kept it light on purpose. The goal is...', 'This doesn’t replace the helpdesk. It just gives...') (Tell 18)
tells_B: Signposting statements announcing what comes next ('Here is what the summary includes.', 'A few notes worth knowing.') (Tell 2)
Frequent lists of three across paragraphs (Tell 6)
